title: What most launch posts skip
subtitle: Operator-level details from TypeSafe docs that change how you build — not the latency screenshot.
source_note: Grounded in docs.typesafe.ai (models, primitives, confidence, jaggedness, how-to-build) and the 15 Sep 2026 System One announcement.

items.title: Jev is a function call, not a chatbot
items.summary: Unstructured state in, typed probabilistic decisions out. It cannot write prose, code, or explanations. Pair it with a generative model when you need language.
items.detail: System One models give up string generation on purpose. The output space is the schema you sent. There is nothing to parse, so there is nothing to hallucinate off-schema. If you find yourself chaining Choices to spell words, stop — that is a generative job.
items.action: Keep control flow in code. Call Jev only where a knowledgeable person would make a snap judgment.

items.title: Everything is Choice, Score, or Noul
items.summary: Choice picks one option (up to 255) with a full distribution. Score sits on an ordered rubric and can land between levels. Noul is P(yes) from 0 to 1 — and has no separate confidence field.
items.detail: Question IDs are for your code; they are not sent to the model. Write the complete question in instructions even when the ID seems obvious. Mix types freely in one request. A Noul of 0.5 is uncertainty, not a medium score — use Score when you need a spectrum.
items.action: Pick the type whose answer your code can branch on directly.

items.title: Ask every question you might need in one call
items.summary: Questions over the same state run in parallel. Adding a speculative question is almost free. The parallel-questions cookbook is ~12× cheaper and ~10× faster than 13 serial calls.
items.detail: State is ingested once. Coding agents default to one question per call — fight that habit. Ignore answers you do not need. Only make a second request when the next question's options or state literally cannot be built until the first answer exists.
items.action: Fan out. Combine in code. Second round-trips are the exception.

items.title: Output tokens are free. Input is $0.042 / MTok
items.summary: $42 per billion input tokens. Output is too cheap to meter. There is no 200k-style cliff on Jev 1.13 — the constraint is a 64k request budget (32k for state + longest question).
items.detail: Rate limits start at 250k tokens/s and 1,200 rpm and can move without notice during early access. SDKs retry 429/529 with backoff. Pin jev-1.13.0 if you have tuned thresholds; jev-latest moves when a new release ships.
items.action: Optimize for question quality and state size, not output length.

items.title: Confidence is a second axis — and Noul does not have one
items.summary: Choice and Score return confidence derived from how peaked the distribution is. Noul's only signal is the probability itself. Do not copy a Noul threshold onto a Choice.
items.detail: High confidence → act. Medium → confirm. Low → human or a slower model. Raise the bar for irreversible actions. TypeSafe is explicit that P(noul) and 1−P(not noul) are not guaranteed to sum to 1, and a Noul is not interchangeable with a yes/no Choice.
items.action: Put thresholds in one file. Match them to risk. Plot confidence vs accuracy on your data.

items.title: Code owns the workflow. Jev is a smart if-statement
items.summary: TypeSafe is for AI-powered software, not agents that choose their next action. Deterministic rules, arithmetic, retrieval, and side effects stay in code.
items.detail: Decompose broad judgments into atomic questions. Weight and combine answers in code so policy can change without a new prompt. For learned composition, feed probabilities into a classical model (see AutoResearch). Do not put an agent while-loop around Jev unless a person is watching.
items.action: Write the software first. Insert System One only where common sense is required.

items.title: Jev 1.13 is literal, and it cannot count
items.summary: It answers the question you wrote, not the one you meant. Keep math, counting, and date arithmetic in code. Filter state before you send it — unrelated context costs accuracy.
items.detail: Known jagged edges: literal reading, numeric precision, date comparison, multi-hop indirection, adversarial state, contradictory instructions vs criteria, and generation. Hex colors underperform named colors. Do not interpolate an exact number from a Score between two levels.
items.action: Read the jaggedness page before production. Test boundary cases. Extraction is a judgment; arithmetic is not.

items.title: You cannot fine-tune Jev. You shape it per request
items.summary: No LoRA, no per-account weights. Put proprietary records in state. Put domain rules in instructions and criteria. Decompose and combine in code.
items.detail: The same RLCD-trained weights serve every account. TypeSafe says customer requests are not used for training. Enterprise ZDR is a legal/plan feature, not a model switch. If you have tuned thresholds, pin the versioned model id.
items.action: Invest in question design and state hygiene, not in a custom checkpoint.

items.title: Jev decides. A generative model writes
items.summary: Use Jev to classify, route, score, guardrail, re-rank, and verify. Use a chat/coding model to draft, explain, and implement. That split is the product.
items.detail: Cookbooks already show the pattern: screen RAG passages before they reach the answering model; check citations against the source; guardrail jailbreaks on the way in and out; pick one skill from a catalog; verify a tool-call trace atomically. Doom and Wikiracing are real-time demos of the same idea.
items.action: Put Jev on the decision path. Keep Grok / GPT / Claude on the generation path.

items.title: English-first, text-only, structured state wins
items.summary: No image/audio/video input. Pre-process binaries to text. Point questions at nested fields with backticked paths like `ticket.messages[0].text`.
items.detail: English is the primary training language. Other languages including CJK are handled but not equally well — watch confidence. Send only the fields the questions need. Large states full of distractors are a documented accuracy drop.
items.action: Retrieve and filter in code, then send a small JSON state with explicit paths in instructions.
